definition.text: The ability of a soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, giving plants a habitat and steady, high-quality yields.

facts.text: A fertile soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and proportions, and is free of toxic substances, such as Fe2+, that inhibit growth.

Contributing properties include enough depth for roots and stored water, good internal drainage and aeration, organic-rich topsoil, nutrients in plant-available forms and microorganisms that support plant growth.
A soil pH between 5.5 and 7.0 suits most plants, though some prefer or tolerate more acid or alkaline conditions.

Fertility rests on constant cycling of nutrients between organic and inorganic forms: microbes decomposing plant and animal wastes release inorganic nutrients, while microbes competing with plants tie them up.
Negatively charged clay and humus hold nutrient cations such as potassium and many micronutrients by cation exchange, which strongly influences fertility.
On farmed land, keeping fertility usually requires soil conservation, because erosion and other degradation lower soil quality.
Growing crops does not by itself exhaust a soil if mineral weathering replaces the nutrients exported in harvests; improper irrigation and acid rain can still deplete it.
Colonial land practices, slavery, and the rise of intensive farming and forestry have all damaged soil fertility and quality.

title: Soil fertilization

definition.text: Adding the nutrients a soil most often lacks for crops, above all phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, the three elements every commercial fertilizer analysis lists.

facts.text: Bioavailable phosphorus is the element most often lacking in soil, especially in humid tropical soils; nitrogen and potassium are also needed in substantial amounts.
Inorganic fertilizers need less labour and carry more concentrated nutrients than organic ones, and since plants take up N, P and K in inorganic forms, they act at once.
Over-reliance on inorganic fertilizers upsets the soil's nutrient balance, lowering soil quality and organic matter, raising erosion risk, and letting soluble nitrate pollute water.
Slow-release fertilizers can cut nutrient leaching and spread the supply of nutrients over a longer period.

notes: The section's claim that chemical fertilizers cause chronic disease in humans (S:a5f4e2c4e1ca) is uncited and was not used.

definition.text: The decline of a soil's fertility when the components that make it fertile are removed and not replaced, and the conditions that support fertility are not maintained.

facts.text: Depletion leads to poor crop yields and is becoming a global problem.
In farming it stems from overly intensive cultivation and poor soil management, including over-tillage, overuse of nutrient inputs that mines the soil's nutrient bank, and salinization.
Rapid changes in land use can severely challenge soil fertility.
As of 2008 depletion was among the most widespread problems in tropical zones, where soils are low in nutrients.
In the Middle East, drought, soil erosion and lack of irrigation hamper farming, with the steepest productivity declines in hilly and dryland areas.
Fertile soil is being depleted across much of Africa, notably the Sahel under high population pressure, and farmers use artificial and natural fertilizers to restore nutrients.
Topsoil depletion, the erosion or exhaustion of organic topsoil that takes hundreds to thousands of years to form, has been blamed for the collapse of many past civilizations.

title: Colonial soil depletion
article: Soil fertility#Colonial impacts on soil depletion

definition.text: The loss of soil fertility caused by colonial settlers' land practices, such as free-ranging livestock, unmanured fields and heavy burning in colonial New England.

facts.text: Colonists in New England let herd animals roam, did not return manure to the soil, and set off a sequence of events that led to erosion.
Historian William Cronon blamed forest removal, more destructive floods, compaction and close-cropping by grazing animals, and ploughing for the increased erosion.
Settlers unfamiliar with Indigenous farming burned land intensively and turned cattle loose to save labour, ruining fertility and preventing sustainable cropping.
About one-half of the Great Plains' original topsoil has disappeared since farming began there in the 1880s, as the Dust Bowl showed.

definition.text: The exhaustion and abandonment of land on Southern slave plantations, whose owners sought to maximize the labour extracted rather than the output per acre.

facts.text: Historian David Silkenat explains that Southern plantation owners treated the landscape as disposable and enslaved Africans as expendable.
After forcing enslaved people to clear forests, planters abandoned the worn land and moved on to more fertile ground.
Draining swamps, clearing forests for monocropping and steamship fuel, and introducing invasive species left eroded hillsides, rivers clogged with sterile soil and extinct native species.

definition.text: The idea, championed by Albert Howard, that the health of crops, livestock and people begins with a fertile, well-kept soil.

facts.text: Albert Howard is credited as the first Westerner to publish Native techniques of sustainable agriculture.
In 1945 Howard wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil, and called soil fertility the basis of the public health system of the future.
He argued that industrial agriculture upsets the balance of nature and irrevocably robs the soil of its fertility.

definition.text: How the quality of irrigation water, and how well it drains away, maintains, degrades or improves a soil's fertility and tilth.

facts.text: About 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated today.
Highly alkaline irrigation water builds up sodium salts that ruin drainage, so roots cannot penetrate deeply into the resulting alkali soils.
Acidic irrigation water drains away useful Ca, Mg, K, P and S and dissolves aluminium and manganese salts that impede plant growth.
Saline water, or poor drainage of irrigated land, turns soil saline and infertile, and saline water also hinders roots' uptake of water and nutrients.

definition.text: The study of the chemical elements and compounds plants need for growth, reproduction and metabolism, and of how they are supplied.

facts.text: An element counts as essential if without it the plant cannot complete a normal life cycle, or if it is part of an essential plant constituent or metabolite.
Plants take carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water, but most other nutrients, nitrogen included, come from the soil.
The elements sit in the soil as salts, so plants absorb them as ions.
Most soils can fully nourish the plants adapted to them, but cropped soil needs fertilizer to sustain yields, since nutrient deficiency limits growth even with ample water and light.
Aristotle and later investigators puzzled over what plant nutrients were and how plants absorbed and transported them.
Justus von Liebig proved in 1840 that plants need nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus.
In 1939 Arnon and Stout grew plants without soil to show that molybdenum is essential to tomatoes.
Nutrients must be available in suitable ratios as well as sufficient amounts, and needs vary between species and even between individuals of one clone.

definition.text: How plants take essential elements in through their roots, above all the root hairs, and pass them to the conducting tissues.

facts.text: Root hairs pump hydrogen ions into the soil; these displace cations held on negatively charged soil particles, freeing them for uptake.
Ions travel to the stele at the root's centre to reach the xylem and phloem, while the Casparian strip blocks passive flow and so regulates what enters.
Uptake works by simple diffusion of nonpolar molecules, facilitated diffusion through transport proteins, and active transport against a concentration gradient using ATP-powered pumps.
In the root apoplast, H+ is exchanged for other cations, and bicarbonate and hydroxide for nutrient anions.
The structure and architecture of the root can change the rate of nutrient uptake.
Because uptake is an active metabolic process, waterlogging, compaction, extreme soil temperatures and poor sugar supply to roots can inhibit it.
Symbioses with nitrogen-fixing rhizobia and with mycorrhizal fungi, which enlarge the effective root surface, both enhance nutrient uptake.

title: Macronutrients and micronutrients

definition.text: The division of plant nutrients into macronutrients, taken up in relatively large amounts, and micronutrients, needed only in small amounts.

facts.text: The soil supplies the macronutrients nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur in relatively large amounts.
Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and carbon together make up over 95% of a plant's dry biomass.
Micronutrients occur in plant tissue at 0.1 to 200 ppm, under 0.02% of dry weight.
The micronutrients are iron, boron, chlorine, manganese, zinc, copper, molybdenum and nickel.
The terms describe how much plants need, not how abundant an element is in the soil.
Soil laboratories group nutrients as major (N, P, K), secondary (S, Ca, Mg) and minor (Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, Mo, Cl).
Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are the elemental macronutrients of all organisms.

notes: Plant nutrition's 'Functions of nutrients' lists cobalt among soil-supplied micronutrients (S:4d364e9a9324) while its lead lists nickel instead (S:806541096d73); the fact uses the lead's list.

definition.text: Iron, a micronutrient plants need to make chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

facts.text: Iron is an enzyme cofactor in photosynthesis and electron transport; it is not part of chlorophyll but is essential for making it.
Deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis and necrosis, and can stem from excess heavy metals or lime in the soil, or from copper deficiency.
Iron(II) is the most useful form because it is more soluble at neutral pH, though plants can also use iron(III) through the photo-reduction of ferric citrate.
In the field, iron fertilizer is supplied as a chelate.

definition.text: Boron, a micronutrient that affects flowering, fruiting, pollen germination, cell division and the forming of cell walls.

facts.text: Boron cannot move in the phloem, so it must reach growing parts through the xylem; deficiency kills terminal growing points and stunts growth.
It is available between pH 5.0 and 7.5 and is mobile in soil, so leaching removes much of it from sandy soils but little from silt or clay.
Decomposing organic matter leaves boron in the topmost soil layer, so deficiency diseases appear in dry weather, when plants cannot draw on that drying layer.
More than one ppm boron in the soil solution is toxic to most plants; toxic soils are mostly limited to arid regions.

definition.text: Zinc, a micronutrient required by a large number of plant enzymes and essential to DNA transcription.

facts.text: Zinc deficiency stunts leaves into 'little leaf', caused by oxidative breakdown of the growth hormone auxin, and stacks leaves together by shortening internodes.
Zinc is the most widely deficient micronutrient in industrial crop production, followed by boron.
Heavy phosphate applications can cause zinc deficiency by forming insoluble zinc phosphates, though soil pH can modify the effect and sometimes raise zinc availability.
Copper and zinc reduce each other's uptake, and zinc also affects a plant's iron levels.

definition.text: How readily a nutrient can be moved within a plant from older tissues to where it is most needed.

facts.text: Plants send nutrients preferentially to their younger leaves rather than their older ones.
Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are mobile, so their deficiencies show first on the oldest leaves.
Nitrogen moves in the xylem as nitrate or organic compounds and in the phloem as amides, amino acids and ureides.
Calcium is immobile in the phloem and arrives only with transpiration through the xylem, so its deficiency shows in new growth.
Boron and sulfur cannot be remobilized from older leaves either, so their deficiencies appear first in the youngest tissues.
Where symptoms appear on a plant therefore helps diagnose which nutrient it lacks.

definition.text: The effects on a plant of too little of an essential nutrient, ranging from slightly slower growth to stunting, deformity, discoloration and death.

facts.text: Visual symptoms distinctive enough to identify a deficiency are rare, since most deficiencies are multiple and moderate; nitrogen is most often the nutrient in shortest supply.
Nitrogen deficiency brings stunted, slow growth and chlorosis, sometimes with purple stems and leaf undersides from anthocyanin.
Phosphorus deficiency is hard to diagnose: crops can starve without obvious signs, though leaves may turn intensely green, reddish or purple.
Calcium deficiency weakens root systems and causes blossom end rot in tomatoes, peppers and watermelons, bitter pit in apples and black heart in celery.
Potassium deficiency causes necrosis or interveinal chlorosis, wilting, more disease and greater frost and heat damage, starting in older tissues.
Iron, manganese and copper deficiencies show on new growth, molybdenum on older growth, zinc on old and new leaves, and boron on terminal buds.
Chlorosis is not always a nutrient problem: solarization looks similar, but unlike deficiency it causes no early leaf drop.

definition.text: Harm to a plant from a nutrient present at too high a level.

facts.text: Deficiency of one element can look like toxicity from another, and an abundance of one nutrient can cause deficiency of another.
Excess soluble boron, molybdenum and chloride are toxic.
Boron above 1 ppm in soil water is toxic to most plants; within plants, 10 to 50 ppm is toxic for small grains, while tolerant crops such as sugar beets withstand 200 ppm.
A fertile soil lacks toxic substances such as Fe2+, which causes nutrient toxicity.

definition.text: The ways the supply of one nutrient affects the uptake, movement or action of another in plants.

facts.text: Calcium and magnesium inhibit uptake of trace metals, and copper and zinc reduce each other's uptake; such effects depend on species and growing conditions.
Potassium uptake can be influenced by the amount of ammonium available.
Potash fertilizers can reduce uptake of phosphorus, magnesium and calcium, so imbalanced potassium fertilizing can markedly lower yields.
Heavy nitrogen applications on sulfur-poor fields can cause sulfur deficiency by dilution, as faster growth raises the plant's sulfur demand.

title: Plant tissue analysis

definition.text: Chemical analysis of plant tissue to describe a plant's nutrient status, also called its ionome or nutrient profile.

facts.text: Interpreting such analyses has been controversial.
In recent decades, mathematical models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced the nearly two-century-old Liebig's law in this work.
Plant tissue tests can identify nitrogen deficiencies, and sensing chlorophyll content allows variable nitrogen rates during the season.
Analysing plant material can reveal boron deficiency early enough to correct it before symptoms appear, after which crop loss cannot be prevented.

contested_note: The source calls the interpretation of plant tissue analyses controversial.

title: Hydroponics

definition.text: Growing plants in a water-nutrient solution instead of nutrient-rich soil or substrate.

facts.text: The most common nutrient solution, developed by D. R. Hoagland and W. C. Snyder in 1933, holds all essential macro- and micronutrients in the proportions most plants need.
Aerators prevent hypoxia, which inhibits root respiration and so nutrient uptake.
In the nutrient film technique, a thin film of nutrient solution flows past roots that are not fully submerged, keeping them aerated.

notes: The Hydroponics article was crawled but is out of scope; the entry is anchored on the Plant nutrition section.

title: Luxury consumption

definition.text: Uptake by a plant of more of a nutrient than healthy growth needs, as happens with potassium when soil levels are high.

facts.text: Macronutrients, normally 0.15% to 6.0% of plant dry matter, are sometimes taken up beyond need, especially when fertilizer is applied in excess.
Calcium uptake was long regarded as luxury consumption but is now considered essential, for cell walls and membranes among other roles.
Potassium uptake rises with root temperature and depresses calcium uptake.

notes: No article or section of its own; mentioned on Plant nutrition, Plant nutrients in soil and Fertilizer.

definition.text: The chemical elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle; sixteen are usually listed as essential for growth and reproduction.

facts.text: They are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium, iron, boron, manganese, copper, zinc, molybdenum and chlorine.
Apart from C, H and O, supplied by carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen, supplied by nitrogen fixation, all come originally from the soil's mineral fraction.
Plants can take up a nutrient only in a plant-available form, mostly as ions absorbed from the soil water.
Most nutrients are locked in primary and secondary minerals that weather too slowly for rapid growth; ground feldspar or apatite seldom supplies enough potassium or phosphorus.
Nutrients held exchangeably on clay colloids and organic matter form a more accessible reservoir that refills the soil solution as plants draw it down.
Microbial decomposition of organic matter also refills the soluble pool, which matters most for the supply of nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus and boron.
Gram for gram, humus holds far more nutrients and water than clay minerals, and supplies most of a soil's cation exchange capacity.
Under Liebig's law, a nutrient short in the soil solution keeps others from being taken up at the best rate, so a particular nutrient ratio is needed for optimal growth.

conflicts.text: The essential plant nutrients include seventeen elements, the sixteen above plus nickel.
conflicts.note: Plant nutrition (S:b43883e6b99f, S:806541096d73) and Nutrient (S:0a0bcf232228) count 17 by including nickel; Plant nutrients in soil (S:c534a30ab638) and Nutrient management (S:70398b1ef480) count 16, and Plant nutrients in soil lists nickel as non-essential (S:45e22eb1ba05).

definition.text: The movement of dissolved nutrient ions through the soil to root surfaces by mass flow, diffusion and root interception.

facts.text: Nutrients touching a root are used up within about 2 mm, so most ions must travel some distance through the soil solution.
In mass flow, dissolved nutrients are carried with the water moving toward a transpiring root, like leaves floating down a stream.
In diffusion, ions move by random motion from richer soil toward the depleted zone at the root surface, and it continues even when closed stomata halt mass flow.
Root interception, the slowest mechanism, works as roots grow into new, undepleted soil.
For corn, mass flow is estimated to supply 98.8% of nitrogen and 95.0% of sulfur, while diffusion supplies 90.9% of phosphorus and 77.7% of potassium.
Phosphorus and potassium depend on diffusion because roots absorb them so fast that their concentration next to the root falls almost to zero.
Decomposing organic matter, which holds 90–95% of soil nitrogen and sulfur and 20–75% of soil phosphorus, supplies much of plants' anion nutrients.
Where crops are grown, natural replenishment of the soil solution usually has to be topped up with fertilizer or organic matter.

title: Carbon in plant nutrition

definition.text: The supply of carbon to plants, taken mainly as carbon dioxide from the air through photosynthesis.

facts.text: About 45% of a plant's dry mass is carbon.
Plants also take dissolved carbon from the soil solution and receive carbon through mycorrhizal networks.
At its normal 0.03% in air, CO2 can limit growth when water and nutrients are not scarce, and raising CO2 strongly promotes growth up to levels above 300 ppm.
Soil air holds 10 to 100 times the atmospheric CO2 concentration, which can reach toxic levels when porosity is low or flooding blocks diffusion.

notes: Also draws on Soil fertility#Light and CO2 limitations (S:51ad58a680bf).

definition.text: Nitrogen, the most critical element plants draw from the soil, taken up as the ammonium cation or the nitrate anion.

facts.text: Nitrogen compounds make up 40% to 50% of the dry matter of protoplasm, and nitrogen is part of amino acids, proteins and chlorophyll.
It is the most critical nutrient plants take from soil and often limits growth, except in tropical rainforests, where phosphorus is the limiting soil nutrient.
Air is nearly 79% N2, but its triple bond makes it almost inert, so it must be fixed as ammonium or nitrate before plants can use it.
Most soil nitrogen is bound in organic matter and must be mineralized to ammonium or nitrate, though mycorrhizal fungi give plants access to some organic nitrogen.
Net mineralization adds about 50 kg of nitrogen per hectare on average, the main usable source in unfertilized fields.
Bacteria in legume root nodules may add 200 to 300 kg of nitrogen per hectare per year, possibly enough for the crop.
Grassland soils hold more nitrogen than forest soils, cultivation lowers soil nitrogen, and no-till soils keep more than tilled ones.
Plants take up most nitrogen as nitrate, but ammonium dominates in acid environments such as boreal forests, where nitrification is less likely.

definition.text: The escape of usable nitrogen from soil through leaching of nitrate, denitrification and ammonia volatilization.

facts.text: Nitrate leaches easily, unlike ammonium, and pollutes groundwater or runoff, especially under heavy fertilizer use.
In denitrification, bacteria short of oxygen in poorly aerated soil respire with nitrate, releasing N2 or N2O; it can remove 25 percent of fertilizer and manure nitrogen on heavy clay.
On alkaline soils ammonium turns to ammonia gas, and ammonium fertilizer applied there can lose as much as 87 percent by volatilization.
These losses drive aquifer and air pollution, soil acidification and eutrophication, causing severe biodiversity loss in natural ecosystems.

definition.text: Phosphorus, a primary plant nutrient and, after nitrogen, probably the element most likely to be deficient in soils.

facts.text: In plants it forms DNA, RNA and membrane phospholipids, and as part of ATP it underpins every energy transfer in the cell.
It is often the most deficient nutrient in tropical soils, where leaching and weathering have depleted the mineral pool and, unlike nitrogen, it cannot be replenished from the air.
Total soil phosphorus averages 0.06 percent by weight, mostly in organic forms unavailable until mineralized or passed to plants by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Apatite is the commonest mineral source; dissolved phosphate not quickly taken up forms insoluble calcium phosphates or iron and aluminium hydrous oxides.
Phosphorus is largely immobile in soil, so it is not leached but builds up in the surface layer if not cropped, and it reaches roots mainly by diffusion.
It is most available at pH 6.5 in mineral soils and 5.5 in organic soils.
Mycorrhizae increase phosphorus uptake, and on some soils spruces and other conifers depend on them for it.
Rock phosphate reserves are limited and being depleted by fertilizer use; peak phosphorus is estimated to have occurred in 1988 for the U.S. and 1989 for the world.

definition.text: Potassium, a primary nutrient present in all plant parts that activates enzymes, though it is not built into any major plant constituent.

facts.text: Potassium opens and closes stomata through an ion pump, so it controls water loss from leaves and raises drought tolerance.
It is outstandingly mobile and soluble in plant tissue and activates enzymes of photosynthesis and respiration.
Soils hold 3 to 100 tons of potassium per hectare in the top 20 cm, but only 2 per cent of it is available to plants.
Biotite mica and potassium feldspar are common mineral sources, and rhizobacteria help solubilize potassium with organic acids.
Once dissolved, about half is held as exchangeable cations on clay minerals and half stays in the soil solution.
As soils dry, potassium can be fixed between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite and montmorillonite, up to 90 percent within ten minutes.
It leaches easily from low-clay soils unless manuring or liming offsets their poor cation exchange capacity.
Potassium improves fruit colour, shape and sugar content, so potassium-rich soils yield quality fruit.

definition.text: Calcium, a secondary macronutrient that forms part of plant cell walls and reaches plants as exchangeable ions and moderately soluble minerals.

facts.text: Soil calcium occurs as insoluble calcite and dolomite, as a divalent cation in solution, as exchangeable ions on particle surfaces, and complexed with organic matter.
Being soluble, it leaches, so it runs low in sandy, heavily leached or strongly acidic soils, which then need liming.
It is more available than potassium because calcite dissolves more readily than feldspar, and mass flow alone usually brings enough to roots.
In plants it builds cell walls, aids root development and acts as a messenger in the cytosol.

definition.text: Magnesium, a secondary macronutrient best known as a constituent of the chlorophyll molecule.

facts.text: It activates many enzyme reactions, working closely with energy-supplying phosphorus compounds.
Magnesium is one of the dominant exchangeable cations in most soils, after calcium and potassium.
Weathering of hornblende, biotite and vermiculite releases it; highly weathered and sandy soils may become deficient through leaching by heavy rain.

definition.text: Sulfur, a secondary macronutrient that is part of some amino acids and vitamins and is essential for chloroplasts.

facts.text: Like phosphorus, most sulfur becomes available as decomposing organic matter releases it, so it declines with depth along with organic matter.
Some soils, especially sandy ones, are deficient and need sulfur added when cropped.
Legumes need it to fix nitrogen, and plants need it to turn nitrate into amino acids and protein.
Sulfur cannot be moved out of older leaves, so yellowing and stunting appear first in the youngest tissues.

title: Plant micronutrients

definition.text: Essential elements that plants and other organisms need only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems.

facts.text: In order of importance they include chlorine, iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper and molybdenum.
Every process that supports plant growth is mediated by a protein containing a micronutrient; manganese, for example, builds the structure of photosystem II.
Copper aids photosynthesis and lignin formation, manganese helps build chloroplasts, and chlorine serves osmosis and ionic balance.
Nickel activates urease, the enzyme that processes urea; without it toxic urea builds up and causes necrotic lesions.
Molybdenum is part of nitrate reductase and of nitrogenase, the enzyme of biological nitrogen fixation.
Their original source is rock, which must weather before they cycle; soil minerals generally supply enough, but heavy phosphate use can cause zinc and iron deficiency by forming insoluble phosphates.
Too little uptake causes deficiencies, such as chlorosis from a lack of copper, iron, manganese or zinc, while elevated soil concentrations cause toxicity.
Some micronutrients can be applied as seed coatings, and acidifying nitrogen fertilizers keep micronutrient cations soluble longer in alkaline soils.

notes: Gap-fill: re-anchored from Plant nutrients in soil#Micronutrients to the crawled Micronutrient article (mostly human and ecosystem material; its plant section is used).

title: Beneficial plant elements

definition.text: Elements that improve plant health but whose absence does not stop the life cycle, such as cobalt, strontium, vanadium, silicon and nickel.

facts.text: Silicon is not considered essential, but experiments show it strengthens cell walls and improves drought and frost resistance, lodging and pest defences.
Cobalt does not seem essential for most plants but is essential for nitrogen fixation by bacteria associated with legumes.
Sodium can partly take over potassium's control of the stomata and is essential for C4 rather than C3 plants.
Selenium is probably not essential for flowering plants, but selenium fertilizers raise crop selenium and help animals fed from selenium-deficient soils.

conflicts.text: As their importance is evaluated, such elements may be added to the essential list, as has happened for silicon.
conflicts.note: Plant nutrition says silicon is not considered an essential element (S:264ced5d5fc0).

notes: Nickel is listed here as non-essential (S:45e22eb1ba05) but as an essential micronutrient on Plant nutrition (S:806541096d73); see the conflict on Essential plant nutrients.

definition.text: A substance an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce.

facts.text: Animals, plants, fungi and protists all need nutrients, and different kinds of organism have different essential nutrients.
Plants need a wider range of minerals, absorbed through their roots, plus carbon dioxide and oxygen taken in through their leaves.
Nutrients may be organic, such as proteins, fats, sugars and vitamins, or inorganic, such as iron, selenium and zinc.
An essential nutrient is one an organism needs for normal function but cannot make itself, at all or in sufficient amounts.
Too little of a nutrient is a deficiency, and harm from too much is nutrient toxicity.
Because plants take their minerals from the soil, the minerals in the human diet come from plants eaten directly or from animals that ate them.

title: Liebig's law of the minimum

definition.text: The principle that growth is set not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one, the limiting factor.

facts.text: Carl Sprengel developed it in agricultural science in 1840, and Justus von Liebig later popularized it.
Applied first to crops, it explained why adding more of a plentiful nutrient did not raise growth, while adding the limiting nutrient did.
In soil terms, when one nutrient is short in the soil solution, stoichiometry keeps the plant from taking up the others at an optimal rate.
It has been extended to biological populations and is commonly used in ecosystem models, for factors such as sunlight or nitrate and phosphate.
In the sea, phytoplankton can be limited by iron in nutrient-rich coastal upwellings and by nitrogen and phosphorus in nutrient-poor open ocean.
Diagnosing limiting factors is a common study, but the approach has been criticized, and models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced it in plant nutrition.
In natural resource management it implies that growth is restricted by the scarcest input; phosphorus, having no substitute, will have to be recycled.
Blackman wrote in 1905 that a process governed by several factors runs at the pace of the slowest; disciplines differ on whether several factors can co-limit at once.

contested_note: The limiting-factor approach has been criticized, and plant nutrition has largely replaced it with models of nutrient interactions.

title: Liebig's barrel
article: Liebig's law of the minimum#Liebig's barrel

definition.text: A picture of the law of the minimum: a barrel with staves of unequal length holds water only up to its shortest stave.

facts.text: Dobenecks used the barrel to explain Liebig's law: a plant's growth is limited by the nutrient in shortest supply, as the barrel is by its shortest stave.
Adaptation acts like a cooper lengthening the shortest stave, so well-adapted systems compensate their limiting factor as far as possible.
Hence a paradox: a law of the minimum seen in artificial systems should be violated in nature, where adaptation evens out the load among factors.

definition.text: The ratio of the mass of carbon to the mass of nitrogen in organic residues.

facts.text: In soil it expresses the balance between energy food for microbes, represented by carbon, and protein-building material, represented by nitrogen.
Plant residues typically run from 13:1 to 100:1, from alfalfa at 13 to oat straw at 80; sawdust reaches 250, while bacteria are only 4.
Above 30:1, residues leave microbes short of nitrogen, so they take up soil ammonium and nitrate and immobilize them; below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants.
Excess carbon makes microbes compete with plants for soil nitrogen until the microbes die; excess nitrogen is left behind but may be leached.
A ratio around 24:1 gives high microbial activity, 30:1 is recommended for soil materials, and microbes themselves are about 10:1.
As microbes and soil fauna digest organic matter and release CO2, the C/N falls, and a lower soil ratio correlates with higher productivity.
Compost, manure and mulch can modify a soil's C:N, and a soil test can measure it.

definition.text: Balancing the carbon and nitrogen in compost feedstocks, which matters for compost much as for soil feedstock.

facts.text: Composting microbes prefer a feedstock ratio of 30–35:1, though some carbon, especially lignin, is not fully digested.
An imbalanced ratio slows composting and lowers its temperature; below 15:1, ammonium can outgas, causing odour and nitrogen loss.
Finished compost has a C:N of around 10:1.
Feedstock carbon and nitrogen contents come from lookup tables, and a mixture's ratio is found by summing the carbon and the nitrogen of all components and dividing.

conflicts.text: Composting is most efficient with a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of about 25:1.
conflicts.note: The Compost article gives about 25:1 as the most efficient ratio; Carbon-to-nitrogen ratio says composting microbes prefer 30-35:1 (S:72f7d5a9d31e).

title: Sediment C/N ratio

definition.text: Use of the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of sediments as a proxy for the sources of their organic matter and for past climate.

facts.text: Ratios of 4–10:1 usually mean marine sources, while land vascular plants tend to exceed 20, because algae lack cellulose and hold more protein.
Bacteria preferentially degrade nitrogen-rich matter as it sinks, so the ratio rises with depth, to about 10 at 1000 m and up to 15 below about 2500 m.
In lake cores, abrupt shifts mark changes between algal and land-plant sources, suggesting deep-water or shallow, marshy phases.
CHN analyzers and continuous-flow isotope ratio mass spectrometers measure the ratio.

notes: Peripheral to soil science; kept because it is a section of a seed page.

title: Soil test

definition.text: A laboratory or in-situ analysis to determine the chemical, physical or biological characteristics of a soil.

facts.text: The most widely run soil tests estimate plant-available nutrient concentrations to guide fertilizer recommendations.
An agricultural test analyses a sample for nutrients, composition and acidity, revealing deficiencies and possible toxicities; it is meant to mimic how roots take up minerals.
Labs such as Iowa State and Colorado State recommend 10–20 sample points per 40 acres of field, and composite sampling mixes soil from several spots.
Nutrients vary with depth and time, so sampling depth and timing affect results; samples are best analysed within about 24 hours, or else frozen or air-dried.
Plant-available phosphorus is measured by chemical extraction, and Europe alone uses more than 10 different tests whose results are not directly comparable.
Some labs analyse all 13 mineral nutrients plus a dozen potentially toxic elements with the 'universal soil extractant', ammonium bicarbonate DTPA.
Do-it-yourself kits usually test only N, P, K and pH and are less accurate than laboratory tests.
In geotechnical engineering, soil tests determine a soil's physical state, seepage, shear strength and deformation properties.

notes: Event: from 2004 laboratories began adding fertilizer recommendations to soil reports (S:c0f743ae7593).

title: Grid soil sampling
article: Soil test#Geographic distribution of samples for precision agriculture

definition.text: Collecting GPS-located soil samples on a regular grid to estimate how nutrients vary across a field.

facts.text: Sample distribution and resolution are chosen to capture the field's spatial variability, weighing the goals of the analysis against the cost of sampling.
In U.S. corn and soybean regions, many providers offer one sample per 2.5-acre grid.
A reference map recording sample locations and quantities is needed to interpret the results.

definition.text: Soil tests in geotechnical engineering that measure physical characteristics such as water content, void ratio and bulk density.

facts.text: They also give information on shear strength, rate of consolidation and permeability.
Examples include grain size analysis by sieve or hydrometer, and constant-head or falling-head permeability tests.

definition.text: Soil testing for lead, a particularly dangerous soil contaminant, to judge the health risk of garden soil.

facts.text: Common mineral soil contaminants include arsenic, barium, cadmium, copper, mercury, lead and zinc.
Children and pregnant women should avoid soil with estimated total lead above 300 ppm; 500–1000 ppm is rated medium and 1000–3000 ppm high.
Advice includes siting gardens away from old painted buildings and busy roads, adding compost, and liming to pH 6.5, which minimizes lead availability.

definition.text: A method, introduced in 2007, that measures the soil nitrogen available to plants by estimating amino sugar nitrogen.

facts.text: It predicts whether adding nitrogen fertilizer will raise crop yields; for corn and soybeans the optimal range is around 225 to 240 mg/kg.
Below that range some nitrogen fertilizer is needed; above it, more nitrogen will not increase yield.
It offers an alternative to the Corn Belt's yield-based method, used since about 1975, of applying 1.1 to 1.4 lbs of nitrogen per bushel of expected corn.
Illinois trials found the yield-based method usually over-applies nitrogen, which is lost to air or water and appears to speed the decomposition of soil organic matter.

definition.text: The science and practice of linking soil, crop, weather and water conditions with farming and conservation practices to use nutrients efficiently for yield, quality and profit while limiting their loss to the environment.

facts.text: It matches the rate, source, timing and placement of nutrients to each field's soil, climate and crop, an approach known as 4R nutrient stewardship.
Managers plan applications for achievable yields, budget all nutrient sources and sinks at the site, and manage soil, water and crop to curb leaching, runoff and volatilization.
Nutrient pathways interact: practices that cut surface runoff of one nutrient may increase leaching of others.
The International Plant Nutrition Institute's 4R manual sets out the right source, rate, time and place for applying nutrients.
Using less nitrogen fertilizer through nutrient management could avoid nitrous oxide emissions equal to 2.77–11.48 gigatons of carbon dioxide from 2020 to 2050.

definition.text: A farm plan that makes all the nutrient sources a crop uses more efficient while lowering production and environmental risk.

facts.text: It is generally agreed to have ten components, beginning with a field map of reference points, acreage and soil types, and a soil test to set nutrient rates.
It also weighs crop sequence, yield estimates from historic records, nutrient sources such as manure, and sensitive areas near streams or wells.
It sets recommended rates, timing and methods, favouring injection where feasible, and is reviewed and updated every year.
For animal feeding operations it may be called a manure management plan; some U.S. agencies require one, and the NRCS publishes guidance on comprehensive plans.

definition.text: Managing applied nitrogen so crops use it as efficiently as possible and as little as possible is lost from the soil.

facts.text: Of the 16 essential nutrients, nitrogen is usually the hardest to manage, because plant-available nitrogen changes quickly with soil water.
Nitrogen escapes by leaching, runoff, erosion, ammonia volatilization and denitrification, and nitrate is the form most at risk.
Careful choice of fertilizer source, rate, timing and placement can cut nitrous oxide emissions per unit of crop by up to half.
Rates should allow for nitrogen mineralized from organic matter and legume residues and supplied in manure, irrigation water and atmospheric deposition.
Applying nitrogen close to crop uptake in split doses reduces losses, as do controlled-release fertilizers and nitrification inhibitors that keep nitrogen as ammonium.
Incorporating or injecting urea and ammonium fertilizers, or adding urease inhibitors, reduces ammonia volatilization.
Cover crops and deep-rooted rotations capture leftover nitrate, while buffers and constructed wetlands strip nitrogen from runoff and drainage water.
Models such as NLEAP and Adapt-N use daily soil, weather and crop data to predict the fate of applied nitrogen.

definition.text: Tests of soil and plants used to judge whether, and how much, nitrogen a crop needs.

facts.text: Preplant soil tests show the soil's nitrogen-supplying power, and late-spring or pre-side-dress tests decide whether more is needed.
Amino sugar tests, grid mapping and real-time sensors can refine nitrogen needs, and post-harvest tests check the previous season's management.
Plant tissue tests identify deficiencies, and post-black-layer corn stalk nitrate tests show whether the last crop got too little, enough or too much nitrogen.

definition.text: The loss of nutrients and micronutrients from a habitat, most often the soil; a form of resource depletion.

facts.text: It ends in nutrient deficiency, and its opposite is eutrophication, or nutrient pollution; both tend to reduce biodiversity.
Because nutrients are the first link in food chains, their loss disturbs nutrient cycling and whole food chains, reaching people as malnourishment.
Growing the same crop with the same fertilizer on the same land every year yields decreasing returns.
Overfarming can turn fertile soil into barren land within a few years.

definition.text: Limited plant growth because a plant cannot take up enough of the essential micronutrient molybdenum from its growing medium.

facts.text: It arises from soils low in molybdenum or from strong sorption that holds it unavailable, sorption being strongest in acid soils; acid sandy soils suffer most.
Molybdenum is needed for nitrogenase, nitrate reductase and xanthine dehydrogenase, so deficient plants accumulate nitrate and legumes fix less nitrogen.
Symptoms include pale leaves with chlorosis and scald, and whiptail in Brassica crops such as cauliflower; leaf contents of 0.2–2.0 mg/kg suffice for most crops.
Liming often relieves it by reducing sorption, but soil, seed or foliar molybdenum fertilizer such as sodium molybdate is often far more cost-effective.

definition.text: Land where plant growth is sparse or stunted and biodiversity may be limited.

facts.text: Toxic or infertile soil, high winds, coastal salt spray and climate are often key causes of poor plant growth.
Serpentine barrens form on soils weathered from ultramafic bedrock, poor in water, nitrogen and phosphorus, yet carry very diverse floras with many endemics.
The Pine Barrens grow on acidic, coarse sands and gravels whose mature soils are siliceous, highly permeable podzols.

title: Law of the Maximum

definition.text: A principle developed by Arthur Wallace that total crop growth is proportional to about 70 growth factors and cannot exceed their aggregate value.

facts.text: Each factor scores from 0 (no growth) to 1 (maximum) and growth is their product: three factors at 0.5 give 12.5% of optimum, three at 0.9 give 72.9%.
In a demonstration, low phosphorus alone gave 83% of optimum growth and low nitrogen 71%; both together gave 57%, close to the predicted 59%.
The factors span nutrient adequacy and toxicities, nutrient interactions, soil conditions such as pH, salinity, texture and aeration, soil biology, weather and management.
Unless limiting factors are corrected, nutrients, water and other inputs are not fully used and are wasted.

notes: Soil test cites it as a model of expected growth. Unlike the law of the minimum, it multiplies all factors rather than taking the scarcest.

definition.text: A plant disorder, also called lime-induced chlorosis, in which a plant gets too little iron to make enough chlorophyll, so its leaves turn yellow.

facts.text: Soil iron may be plentiful yet unavailable when soil pH is above 6.5, and excess elements such as manganese can also block iron uptake.

Yellowing appears between the veins of newly emerging leaves, because iron is not mobile in the plant; raspberries, pears and acid-loving plants such as azaleas and camellias are especially susceptible.
Where soil pH is over seven, it can be lowered toward 6.5–7 with organic matter such as compost or manure, acidifying ammonium sulphate fertilizer, or elemental sulphur, which oxidizes over months.
Iron sulphate or iron chelates supply iron at once: iron sulphate and Fe EDTA work in soil only up to pH 7.1, while Fe EDDHA works up to pH 9.

title: Boron deficiency

definition.text: A shortage of the micronutrient boron in plants, the most widespread micronutrient deficiency, which stops cell expansion, kills growing points and reduces fertility.

facts.text: Soils typically hold an adequate 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg of boron, and deficiency is common below 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, depending on crop and soil.
It strikes high-pH soils, where boric acid stays undissociated and cannot be absorbed, soils under 1.5% organic matter, and leached sandy soils.
Hot spots include leached Ferralsols and Acrisols in Africa, Oxisols of Brazil's Cerrado, and calcareous soils in Pakistan, where 35 to 56 percent of fields are deficient.
Boric acid, borax or Solubor at about 1.1 kg boron per hectare corrects it, but excess is toxic and additions may stay unavailable in alkaline soils.

notes: Lead sentence S:770657ebdf02 calls boron deficiency the most widespread micronutrient deficiency; the Zinc as a plant nutrient entry (Plant nutrition) says zinc is the most widely deficient micronutrient in industrial crop production, followed by boron. Scopes differ, so not logged as a conflict.

definition.text: A plant disorder caused by too little available calcium in the growing medium or, more often, by low transpiration of the plant or the affected tissue.

facts.text: Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first.
Acidic, sandy or coarse soils often hold less calcium, and high-phosphorus soils tend to lock it into insoluble forms.
Typical disorders are bitter pit in stored apples, blossom end rot in tomatoes and peppers, and tipburn in lettuce.
Liming acid soils toward pH 6.5 can help, but adding calcium at the roots seldom cures it, so steady watering is key.

definition.text: A condition in which leaves make too little chlorophyll and turn pale, yellow or yellow-white.

facts.text: A chlorotic plant can make little carbohydrate by photosynthesis and may die unless the cause is treated.
Causes include soil shortages of iron, magnesium or zinc, too little nitrogen, a soil pH that locks up minerals, waterlogging and damaged or compacted roots.
On limestone vineyard soils vines struggle to take up iron; grafting onto American rootstocks after phylloxera made this lime chlorosis worse in France.
Treatments include iron chelate or sulphate, magnesium or nitrogen feeds, lime on acid soils and sulfur on alkaline ones.

definition.text: A plant disorder from too little available manganese, often confused with and occurring alongside iron deficiency.

facts.text: It is most common in poorly drained soils and where organic matter is high, and manganese may be unavailable at high pH.
Leaves yellow between the veins in a chequered pattern; young leaves show it first because manganese is immobile, unlike magnesium deficiency.
Plants need manganese in the four-manganese core of photosystem II's oxygen-evolving complex, so most broad-spectrum fertilizers contain it.
Lowering pH with ammonium sulfate acts at once, while sulfur works slowly through soil bacteria; the US used about 20,000 tons of manganese fertilizer compounds in 2000.

definition.text: Limited plant growth because the plant cannot take up enough of the essential micronutrient zinc from its growing medium.

facts.text: Some soils hold little zinc (sandy soils, Histosols, highly weathered soils); others sorb it strongly (calcareous soils, Vertisols, saline soils); low organic matter and compaction add risk.
Phosphorus fertilizers and liming frequently induce it, the latter by increasing zinc sorption.
Leaf zinc of 20 to 100 mg/kg suffices for most crops; zinc sulphate or oxide at 5 to 100 kg/ha corrects it, though perhaps not in alkaline soils.
Almost half the world's cereal crops grow on zinc-deficient soils, so zinc deficiency in people is widespread.

definition.text: A plant disorder in which a plant cannot obtain enough nitrogen from the soil, causing stunting, poor flowering and fruiting, and chlorosis.

facts.text: Adding high-carbon matter such as sawdust lets soil organisms use up available nitrogen, 'robbing' it from plants.
Older leaves yellow first because the plant moves nitrogen to younger tissue.
Other stresses mimic its symptoms, so it is best confirmed with soil and tissue tests, or chlorophyll meters, since leaf nitrogen tracks chlorophyll.
Winter green manures limit leaching and leguminous ones fix extra nitrogen; urea, ammonium phosphate and calcium ammonium nitrate correct it.

definition.text: A plant disorder caused by an insufficient supply of phosphorus, taken up as phosphate ions.

facts.text: Most soil phosphorus is in forms plants cannot absorb; pH sets the phosphate species, and between pH 6 and 7 the least is bound up.
Deficient plants mature slowly, store excess starch and may turn dark purple from anthocyanin, but discoloration appears only when deficiency is fairly severe.
It is diagnosed mainly by soil tests such as Bray 1-P, Mehlich 3 and Olsen, which extract phosphorus for colorimetric measurement.
Roots respond by favouring lateral roots and secreting phosphatases and organic acids; larger roots and mycorrhizal partners raise uptake.

definition.text: A plant disorder caused by depletion of potassium ions in the soil, also called potash deficiency.

facts.text: It is most common in light, sandy, low-clay soils, since soluble potassium leaches easily from soils lacking colloids.
Leaf tips scorch brown and curl and veins yellow between them, first on older leaves, because potassium is mobile in the plant.
Deficient plants are more prone to frost and disease, though potassium above the optimum adds no extra resistance.
Potassium chloride is the main remedy; dry soil cuts uptake, and liming or raising organic matter can improve retention.

definition.text: A standard hydroponic nutrient solution that supplies every essential plant element, devised by Hoagland and Snyder in 1933.

facts.text: It is among the most popular standard solutions in science, with more than 21,000 citations.
Revisions added ferric chelates to keep iron in solution and in 1938 cut the trace elements to the accepted essentials B, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, Fe and Cl.
Arnon's 1950 revision changed only molybdenum, from 0.048 to 0.011 ppm.
Meant to imitate a nutrient-rich soil solution, its high nitrogen and potassium suit large plants such as tomato and bell pepper.

definition.text: The proportion of the nitrogen present that a plant absorbs and uses.

facts.text: Crops worldwide generally have nitrogen use efficiencies below 50%.
Raising it cuts fertilizer runoff and production costs and increases yield, making farming more sustainable.
Better fertilizers and crop management, selective breeding and genetic engineering can raise it; it can be measured for the plant, the soil, the fertilizer or the ecosystem.

definition.text: Field tests that estimate a crop's nitrogen status from leaf chlorophyll without destroying the sample, faster than laboratory analysis.

facts.text: Nitrogen tracks chlorophyll because each chlorophyll molecule contains four nitrogen atoms.
Absorption meters shine light through a leaf; brands report different units, such as SPAD, but convert, and readings are linear only below 300 mg/m2.
Fluorescence-ratio meters read up to 675 mg/m2 and can measure small, curved or thick samples.
Laboratory tissue tests usually take one to two weeks, so results may arrive after the time to act.

title: Nutrient budget

definition.text: A comparison of the nutrients applied to soil with those taken up by crops, counting all inputs to a farm and all removals.

facts.text: Inputs include fertilizer, rainfall, brought-in supplements and spread effluent; outputs include sold produce, nitrate leaching, volatilization and phosphate runoff.
It warns early of a surplus, which builds up nutrients and loss risk, or a deficit, which depletes reserves and risks deficiency and lower yields.
It is less exact than a financial statement and relies on assumptions such as average nutrient removal coefficients and yield history.
In turf management, variable-rate application balances the budget by fertilizing only where uptake potential is highest, reducing leaching.

notes: Phrase-dossier concept 'Nutrient budgets'; the crawled page Nutrient budgeting is its own article, so it is used instead of null. duplicate of Nutrient budgeting (same article)

title: Mitscherlich's law of physiological relations

definition.text: Alexander Mitscherlich's 1909 law relating crop yield to the quantity of plant food by a logarithmic function.

facts.text: The function is virtually the law of diminishing returns, to which it was compared in 1942.
It recast the limiting-factor idea that Liebig formulated as the law of the minimum and Blackman later discussed.

notes: Phrase-dossier concept 'Mitscherlich equation'; drafted from the Crop yield section, which is the concept's own section.
